graphify.what: What was tested: graphify 0.9.108 (PyPI package `graphifyy`), its code layer only (the graph its parser builds, no model, no document layer), asked through its own `query` command with the seed definition and seed file as start nodes, depth 3 and a budget large enough that graphify cuts nothing (`query-seed-full-d3`, chosen on the tuning split by the grader's rule from 10 shipped configurations). graphify's ordered list of files was packed by the shared packer exactly as for every other arm, so the comparison is about which files graphify picks and in what order. This is one repository, these task kinds, graphify's code layer; it is not a statement about graphify in general.

questions.qualifier: raw question text, no agent, no vocabulary step, printout scored as an item list

headline_text: On the 418 held-out change-completion tasks (T1, 75 commits), graphify's code layer showed 0.564 of the reference files and definitions inside an 8,000-token answer, against 0.700 for the typed graph: a difference of -0.137 (95 % interval -0.188 to -0.088), and by the declared rule the typed graph is "better" (the sign is the same on T1, T2 and T3).

Against scripted search (0.625), the changed-together floor (0.638) and the same-folder floor (0.549) the declared verdict is "inconclusive" each time: -0.061 [-0.129, +0.007], -0.074 [-0.145, -0.003] with the opposite sign on T3, and +0.014 [-0.057, +0.082].

Where the seed file lives decides most of this: on mobile-app seeds (31 commits, 152 tasks) graphify scored 0.638, -0.019 [-0.092, +0.038] from the typed graph and +0.131 [+0.038, +0.215] above scripted search; on backend seeds (45 commits, 236 tasks) it scored 0.472, -0.227 [-0.295, -0.163] below the typed graph and -0.214 [-0.292, -0.142] below scripted search.

Of the 336 T1 reference files that the typed facts connect to the seed only through a route-to-client, table, setting or changed-together link, graphify showed 0 inside 8,000 tokens, the typed graph 66 and scripted search 91; on the remaining 2,226 reference files graphify showed 0.604 of them, the typed graph 0.722 and scripted search 0.613.
graphify's own default answer text (median 2,182 tokens) named 0.344 of the T1 reference files, against 0.447 for the typed graph's 2,000-token answer and 0.360 for scripted search's.

On the 30 held-out code questions, graphify's answer to the question text scored macro F1 0.072 (typed graph 0.745, scripted search 0.645), with answers of median 2,547 tokens against median 31 and 29.5 tokens of final answer for the other two.
graphify.audit_run_verdict: The run was clean and the scoring holds: every primary, every G-1 to G-4 difference and every native-form and question recall number was reproduced to 4 decimals by code that does not load the grader's code or `score.js`. No verdict word changes. Three more shipped graphify options, tried on tuning tasks only, did not beat the frozen configuration by more than one standard error, so the choice among graphify's options does not explain the held-out gap. This is graphify 0.9.108's code layer, on these task kinds, on one repository; it says nothing about graphify in general.
does_not_say: Nothing about tokens: every answer of every arm filled its budget (median 7,999 tokens), and no session was run. The token-saving claims are neither confirmed nor refuted here.
Nothing about the model-read document layer, community labels or the report, where the one independent positive result for graphify sits.
Nothing about an agent using graphify: whether it would call it, re-query, or read fewer files.
Nothing about other repositories, other languages, orientation questions, or graphify versions other than 0.9.108.
what_it_says: graphify's code layer is the same kind of object as the typed code graph of the first test, and on the first test's own tasks it did not find more of the changed files than the arms that test already had. It did not reveal a capability the first test lacked. Its code layer is not why graphify's published numbers look good on this kind of task.

That is consistent with the explanation in `widen/lane-graphify.md`: graphify's headline numbers measure other things (the size of one capped answer against the whole corpus in context with no correctness check, conversational memory, six agent questions on one other repository).
mustnot_against: graphify is worse than scripted search
graphify is no better than listing the folder
graphify's document layer would not help
mustnot_for: graphify is as good as the typed graph on the mobile app
graphify beats scripted search on the mobile app
graphify is equivalent to scripted search or the floors
graphify is better than the same-folder floor
graphify lost only because it lacks route, table and history links
graphify lost only because of our adapter or packer
graphify was tuned as hard as the typed arms
with more tuning it would win
graphify builds its graph faster or smaller than the typed store
This explains why graphify shows good results elsewhere
mustnot_reasons: "graphify does not work." / "graphify is worse in general." / "graphify is worse than grep."
"graphify is worse than scripted search" or "worse than the changed-together floor" (both inconclusive).
"graphify is no better than listing the folder" (inconclusive on the primary; above it on every ranking secondary).
"graphify's token savings are false" or "graphify wastes tokens" (no tokens were measured).
"graphify cannot answer code questions" or "graphify scores F1 0.07 on questions" without "raw question text, no agent, no vocabulary step, printout scored as an item list".
"graphify's document layer would not help" (not run).
"graphify's graph is wrong" (no edge was checked for correctness; only rankings were scored).
"graphify is as good as the typed graph on the mobile app" (8,000 tokens only; lower at 2,000).
"graphify beats scripted search on the mobile app" or "beats both floors there" (fails at 2,000 and 4,000 tokens, on top-10 ranking, and after dropping five commits; subgroup, no verdict).
"graphify is equivalent to scripted search or the floors" ("inconclusive" is not "equivalent").
"graphify is better than the same-folder floor" (not by the declared rule).
"graphify lost only because it lacks route, table and history links" (the gap is -0.134 on tasks that do not need them; this run does not separate link kinds from ranking and tuning).
"graphify lost only because of our adapter or packer" (no mapping loss; the gap survives on packer-free top-10 recall and nDCG; only the rank of the first right file is level).
"graphify was tuned as hard as the typed arms" or "with more tuning it would win" (10 against 60 configurations; neither is shown).
"graphify builds its graph faster or smaller than the typed store" (times not comparable).
"This explains why graphify shows good results elsewhere" or "this confirms graphify's published numbers" (they measure other things).

(section 6, point 1); its figures are from the lane's tuning report, recomputed by the audit.

Three things to read with the table:

- **A small gain for E1 cannot be ruled out.** Its primary interval nearly excludes zero (the lower end
  is -0.0002). On the 46 of these commits that the pilot's own late 50 also holds, it lies wholly above
  zero: +0.0031 [+0.0008, +0.0057]. Either way the gain is at most about +0.006.
- **The placebo's fused interval lies wholly below zero and still reads "matches"**, because the word
  only asks that the interval stay inside the band. Fused at weight 1 the placebo loses 0.0108.
- **Answer level** (the grader's measure on the same 50 commits: how much of the reference answer fits
  in 8,000 tokens). The protocol gives no word there. The simple ranker scores 0.6995; the fused arms

structured.answer_bold: No arm adds to the simple ranker on this repository.
answer_paragraphs: Four knowledge-graph embedding models and one graph-neural encoder were each fused with the simple ranker and compared with it on the 50 later tuning commits. On top-ten precision every fused arm "matches" it: the largest gain is +0.0023 inside the candidate pool and +0.0032 over all code files, where the protocol asked for at least +0.02 before it would say "adds". A real gain of up to about +0.006 in the pool, and about +0.007 over all code files, cannot be ruled out; that is about a third of the bar. Alone, RotatE and TransE match the simple ranker. ComplEx-N3 and CompGCN match inside the candidate pool and are lower over all code files. The routed specialists are lower in both.

Why, from the audit: the models learn well, but mostly they recover the co-change facts they were trained on, which the simple ranker already has. Below those they order the other candidates about as well as rooted PageRank does. Fused with the simple ranker they add no gain that the protocol's +0.02 bar could register; a small one, of about +0.006 in the pool at most, is not ruled out.

heldout.heading: 75 commits, 418 tasks; one run of the frozen arm; described, not judged
heldout.note: It is the same picture as on tuning, with two differences for E1 alone: over all code files it lies below the simple ranker here, and in the pool its interval reaches past -0.02; on tuning it matched in both. The arms of the earlier graph test on these 75 commits (typed graph 0.700, scripted search 0.625, changed-together floor 0.638, same-folder floor 0.549, answer level) are context only: they were packed in another way (ruling 88(g)).

why.text: On stage A's held-out co-change pairs E1 to E4 reach a mean reciprocal rank of 0.68 to 0.75, against 0.28 for PPR. PPR's graph has no co-change edges, so this shows that the models learned the co-change structure, not that they beat a ranker that has it.

why.lead: Mostly they recover what they were trained on.
why.text: Alone, E1 to E4 separate a file's known co-change partners from the other candidates almost perfectly (AUC 0.996 to 1.000). Inside that block they do not follow CO's order (median rank correlation 0.07 to 0.29). Below it their order is moderately correlated with PPR's (0.49 to 0.63 in the pool) and about as accurate: P@10 on candidates without co-change history is 0.196 to 0.213, against PPR's 0.208. It is not the same order.

why.lead: They find little that is new.
why.text: On those candidates no arm beats PPR by a margin this test can see. The refuter's own contrast, with the truth restricted in the same way, gives E1 +0.004 [-0.005, +0.012] and E3 +0.001; E2, E4 and E5 score below PPR. The data do not show that the embeddings carry no information of their own; they show that it is too little to move the top ten.
Outside the protocol's grid (weights 2, 4 and 8, and the arm alone) no arm's gain over the simple ranker exceeds +0.006 in the pool. The room was there: a perfect order would gain +0.119 in the pool.

why.lead: In the pool the fused list can hardly differ from the simple ranker's.
why.text: There are two causes. The fusion the protocol fixed (k = 60) keeps a candidate with co-change history above one without: in the fused tables the co-change candidates hold the top places in 224 to 226 of the 226 tasks where that can be tested. And the selection gave low weights to arms that added nothing. So the fused top ten shares 9.1 to 9.3 of its 10 files with the simple ranker's, and the placebo moves the list as much as the real models do. "Adds" was still reachable: a perfect score put through the same selection takes weight 1 and gains +0.060 [+0.042, +0.079], and a half-informative one +0.036. But that is the most the primary contrast can show, so "matches" rules out a third to a half of the gain that could be reached, not all of it. The pool "matches" is a weak comparison; the arms alone, the unrestricted lists and the weights beyond the grid (points 2 to 4) carry the conclusion.

The routed specialists' shortfall alone lies entirely in the 192 tasks that were routed to two areas. On the 121 tasks routed to one area E5 equals E1 (0.2226 against 0.2219). About 60 % of E5's gap to E1 on the two-area tasks comes from the merge the protocol wrote (item 13): a candidate that only the second specialist knows enters with that one percentile and takes top-ten places at about 5 % precision. The rest is not explained by this test. Candidates that no specialist knows explain at most 0.008 (the bound comes from the re-test of the arms auditor's finding).

structured.why_sources: Points 2 to 5 come from the audit's refuter, who set out to show that "matches" is an artifact. Point 1 comes from the auditors of stage A and of the arms' code, point 6 from the auditor of E5. A second agent re-tested points 2, 5 and 6 and corrected them; the corrected forms are given here. Point 1's figures are the lane's stage-A table, with a caveat from two auditors; points 3 and 4 rest on one agent's computation.
structured.why_summary: on this repository, at this size, the trained embeddings mostly recover the co-change facts they were trained on; below those they order candidates about as well as rooted PageRank, though not in the same order; and fused with the simple ranker they add nothing this test's bar could register (at most about +0.006 in pool P@10, where the protocol asked for +0.02).
limits: The words for an arm alone over all code files are missing
Values that are not finite numbers
The sources of each arm's settings
Other departures that no ruling names
The selection always took the smallest model
The yardstick is not the pilot's
"No score was read before the freeze" is a statement, not a technical fact
structured.limits_intro: None of these changes a figure or a verdict word. Points 3 to 6 come from my own rulings (105 and 108 to 113), which the audit checked; the others were found by the audit. Those marked (re-tested) were confirmed, or confirmed in part, by a second agent.
does_not_say: It is one repository with small graphs (point 8 above), 50 commits, and truth at file level: what a commit edited, not what it needed to read. No agent was run and no tokens were counted.
Not tested: temporal or inductive models, text or code embeddings, rule learners, larger dimensions, a longer history.

**The routed-specialist idea.** This test used folders as areas, RotatE specialists and the merge as the protocol wrote it, on a graph that one model can hold whole. Most of E5's shortfall comes from the merge as written. Routing a seed to its own area cost nothing: the single-area tasks equal E1. The choice of the second area (the documentation-heavy "other" area on 153 of the 313 tasks) and the quality of specialists trained on parts of the graph were not separated. The test says nothing about routing on a graph too large for one model.

**The harness question** (do a graph layer and learned relations cut what an agent has to read?). At this size a learned ranker gives no better list of related files than rooted PageRank plus co-change confidence, which need no training. The earlier measured gain of the typed store over scripted search is a different question and is not touched by this.

structured.to_beat_caveat: These are sizes of index answers measured on recorded lookups. They are not a forecast of tokens saved: whether an agent would stop reading after such an answer needs an agent run.
structured.design_change: The test set exists and the split is fixed, but for CQ1, CQ2 and CQ4 the truth is mostly "read", not "confirmed used", and only 10.6 % of instances replay against a cached snapshot without possible leakage (product 18.3 %). A zero-model replay can score the graph arms against the index-only arms on the snapshot-ok and read-truth instances; the forms with weak truth (CQ1, CQ2, CQ4) need the agent run that use-cases.md R1 names. Keyword search over names, paths and headings is the strongest index-only arm on almost every form, and it is the one to beat.
could_not_measure: Run-to-run drift: the untracked program documents are read at their live content when baseline.js.txt runs, and other sessions keep writing them, so a re-run can move a baseline cell by an instance or two (seen once: 29.6 to 29.5 %).
Containment of the whole needed span: a baseline "hit" means a result points into a truth span (overlap), not that the result covers all of it.

Which lines of a read the agent actually used: confirmation covers only later edits, file:line citations and verbatim quotes; about 9 % of model calls carry visible text (use-cases.md section 11), so "read but not confirmed" is not "unused".
The exact code version: transcripts carry no commit; the version is the branch tip at the episode time (main when the branch no longer exists), and uncommitted working-tree changes are invisible.

Program documents outside version control: they can only be indexed at their current content, which may hold text written after the session (counted per form as needs-current-docs, and per baseline as hits on current-only files).
Truth outside the repository (scratchpad files, transcripts, memory, web): no repository index can return it; these instances are counted, not scored.
Whether an agent given the index result would have stopped reading: the baselines score containment of the truth span among the first 10 results and its token cost, not the agent behaviour.
Program question forms are labelled by rules that a manual check found right on about 3 in 4 calls (use-cases.md section 2.4); "earlier lane findings" (CQ1) is the noisiest label.
Confirmation-part numbers: the baselines were computed on the development part only, by design; nothing on the confirmation part has been scored.
Product work is 13 main sessions of one day (2026-11-13) and one plan; the development part holds 8 of them and the confirmation part 5. A per-form product number rests on few sessions.

structured.what_it_measures: The graph v2 design wants to store agents' conclusions with the premises they rest on, and re-check a stored conclusion by re-checking its premises. The refuter (`../REFUTE.md`, objection at line 87 and the open item at line 204) said most earlier conclusions in this program rest on things outside version control, so a premise check cannot reach them. This folder measures how true that is. It also measures how often findings are read again and whether a finding that had gone stale was read and used.

step4: **Can keep honest (about 12 to 20 % of these findings):** query-plus-answer findings about this repository (seed values, config defaults, build profiles, call sites), and summaries of tracked spans whose span hash can be re-checked (E1 to E3). Two of the seven query findings went stale within two weeks; a ledger re-running "default of the ping backdate ceiling setting" and "does login compare a PIN with a default" at the new commit would have flagged both, and both still sit unflagged in tracked documents.

**Could keep honest if written differently (up to about half):** script results (M, 25 %) and findings citing untracked notes, scratch files or clinic files. With every cited file content-hashed at citation time, 53 % (41 to 65 %) would have only file or query premises (the change detected, not the conclusion re-derived).

**Cannot:** findings resting on outside sources (25 %), on one-off measurements whose inputs are gone (22 %), and the judgement layer (63 % carry some bare judgement; 68 % are interpretation). For these a ledger can store the date, author and premises, and show their age; it cannot say the conclusion still holds.

**What recording premises at writing time would have required:** about 3 to 4 premise records per finding (median 3, up to 10). In this sample a writer would have had to record, per 100 premises: 6 repository queries, 11 tracked spans with commit, 14 plus 10 plus 8 file spans needing a content hash (repository folder, scratch, clinic), 11 plus 1 clinic git facts, 2 pinned library spans, 12 outside-source citations with fetch date, 7 measurement inputs that were not kept, and 18 judgements to be marked as such.

**What would have to change in how findings are written:** put the query in words or code and the commit beside each code claim; keep measurement inputs and outputs under content hashes (or commit them) instead of in scratch; commit or hash the evidence notes a finding cites; mark judgement as judgement; and give each finding an id the ledger can index. None of this was measured as a cost; it is what the sample says is missing.
